papers.title_in_file: AutoQResearch: LLM-Guided Closed-Loop Policy Search for Adaptive Variational Quantum Optimization
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, hardware-validation discussion, Section VII.D scope and limitations, conclusion; MIS and CVRP result sections read only via the summary sentences.
papers.what_it_is: An LLM-guided closed-loop framework that searches for adaptive solver-control policies for variational quantum optimization, tested on MIS and CVRP.

assertions.value: The authors report that on MIS instances from 16 to 64 vertices the discovered policies substantially outperform the static baseline, and that warm-start QAOA transfers well at 16 nodes but collapses at 32.
quotes: On MIS instances from 16 to 64 vertices, the discovered policies substantially outperform the static baseline and reveal clear scale-dependent solver behavior
warm-start QAOA transfers well at 16 nodes but collapses at 32
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study, in noiseless simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that cheap scout evaluations can misestimate policy quality and even invert candidate rankings, so staged confirmation is part of the method.
quotes: cheap scout evaluations can misestimate policy quality and even invert candidate rankings
assertions.certainty_reason: Log-derived ablation from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that they do not yet isolate the contribution of the LLM from that of the curated surface and staged harness, and that policies are discovered under idealized noiseless simulation.
assertions.anchor: Section VII.D, Scope, Limitations, and Future Directions
quotes: we do not yet isolate the contribution of the LLM from that of the curated surface and staged harness
policies are discovered under idealized noiseless simulation
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limits in Section VII.D.
assertions.reader_inference: No matched-budget comparison against random search, Bayesian optimization or bandits is reported, so the LLM's added value is not established.

assertions.value: The authors state that the hardware validations are restricted single-instance studies, each executed within a single calibration window and reported as a single execution.
quotes: these are restricted single-instance studies and should not be interpreted as broad hardware benchmarks
each was executed within a single calibration window and reported as a single execution
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limits in the hardware validation section.

papers.title_in_file: Shot-frugal and Robust quantum kernel classifiers
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction and contributions, Section VI summary and outlook; derivations and appendices not read in full.
papers.what_it_is: A theory-and-simulation paper bounding the measurement shots a quantum kernel SVM needs for reliable classification and giving shot-frugal robust SVM programs.

assertions.value: The paper proves (Theorem 2), using concentration bounds of subgaussian distributions, a lower bound on the number of measurement shots above which the stochastic kernel classifier has a classification error bounded by the margin error of the exact kernel classifier.
quotes: Theorem 2 characterizes the number of measurement shots needed to reliably reproduce the labels of an ideal classifier (EKC) over any dataset.
Based on concentration bounds of subgaussian distributions, Theorem 2 gives a lower bound Nsg
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 2, Section IV; stated in Section I.B and VI.

assertions.value: The authors report that the robust ShofaR programs reproduce the exact kernel classifier with far fewer measurement shots than the nominal SVM, and show significant savings in Table III, even though the nominal SVM was given the exact training kernel matrix.
assertions.anchor: Section I.B contributions, items 2 and 3; Table III
quotes: which reliably reproduces EKC with far fewer measurement shots than would be needed for the nominal SKC

We compare the performance of all these programs to the nominal PRIMAL SVM and show significant savings (see Table III), even though the nominal SVM was given access to the exact training kernel matrix.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation results on benchmark datasets from one study; the table values are not in the quotes.
assertions.reader_inference: Savings are shown on small synthetic datasets (circles, moons and similar), not on a hardware run.

assertions.value: The authors state that the main results assume an exact (noiseless) training kernel matrix and consider only fundamental sampling noise, with depolarizing noise treated in an appendix.
quotes: The training kernel matrix is assumed to be exact (noiseless training phase
Our results in the article have considered only the fundamental sampling noise
assertions.certainty_reason: Section I.B and Section VI state the scope of the main results.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Section III numerical experiments (setup and result discussion), Section IV conclusion; derivation of the cost function skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A distributed variational quantum algorithm for large linear systems, with the matrix split across several NISQ computers, tested in simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that numerical quantum simulations show the distributed algorithm can solve linear systems whose size scales with the number of computers, so it is not limited by the capacity of a single quantum computer.
quotes: Numerical quantum simulations demonstrate that the proposed distributed quantum algorithm can solve linear systems whose size scales with the number of quantum computers
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation results from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in a simulated Ising-inspired linear system, only the proposed algorithm showed a sustained and rapid decrease in the global residual norm, which fell by more than two orders of magnitude, while three variants without gradient tracking or Adam did not; results are averaged over 10 random initializations.
assertions.anchor: Section III-C and Appendix C, Fig. 3
quotes: only the proposed algorithm exhibits a sustained and rapid decrease in the global residual norm
The residual decreases by more than two orders of magnitude from its initial value
the reported results are averaged over 10 random initializations
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation result on one test system.

assertions.value: The authors state that the current simulation environment does not fully capture realistic noise sources, and that running the algorithm on real quantum hardware is the most important next step.
assertions.anchor: Section III, discussion before Section IV
quotes: The current simulation environment does not fully capture realistic noise sources, including device-dependent gate errors, decoherence, and readout noise.
The most important next step is to implement and evaluate the proposed algorithm on real quantum hardware
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated by the authors in the closing discussion of Section III.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Algorithms in a Superposition of Spacetimes
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Section 1 introduction including 1.3 Results and contributions; technical overview, proofs and appendices not read.
papers.what_it_is: A theoretical paper defining a complexity class with an order-interference oracle motivated by quantum gravity, and placing Graph Isomorphism and a gap closest vector problem in it.

assertions.value: The paper proves that Graph Isomorphism and a Gap Closest Vector Problem variant lie in BQP^OI, the class of problems solvable in polynomial time with bounded error by a quantum algorithm with access to an order interference (OI) oracle.
quotes: BQPOI is defined as the class of problems for which there exists a quantum algorithm with access to an OI oracle, such that the algorithm solves the problem (with bounded error) running in polynomial time in the input size.
We prove the following theorems.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorems 1.1 and 1.2, Section 1.3, proved in Sections 5 to 7.
assertions.reader_inference: The result concerns a hypothetical oracle model, not any existing hardware.

assertions.value: The author states the model is a first example of a natural computational model based on quantum gravity that gives an exponential speedup over standard quantum computation, under standard hardness assumptions.
quotes: an exponential speedup over standard quantum computation (under standard hardness assumptions).
assertions.certainty_reason: The author's summary claim in the abstract; it rests on the relaxed order-interference model and on standard hardness assumptions.

assertions.value: The author states that the precise computational power of BQP^OI is an open question and that no trivial way was found to solve problems complete for NP or SZK.
quotes: We find the precise computational power of BQPOI as an interesting open question.
we did not find a trivial way to solve computational problems that cause major implications to the theory of computational complexity
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated by the author in Section 1.3.

assertions.value: The author states that solving the Gap Closest Vector Problem at the relevant gap means solving the Learning With Errors problem, whose hardness is the central pillar of post-quantum cryptography.
quotes: the Learning With Errors (LWE) problem [Reg09], the computational hardness of which is the central pillar of post-quantum cryptography
assertions.certainty_reason: A background statement the paper attributes to the literature.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Section IV results and discussion (text; tables not extracted), Section V conclusion; methods section skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A Kipu Quantum paper on quantum feature maps from quench dynamics of a spin glass on D-Wave annealers, used to enhance classical ML on three datasets.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the molecular toxicity dataset AQFM-GB gave a performance increase of at least 40% over the baseline GB model, and that on myocardial infarction tasks improvements exceeded 100% in recall for atrial fibrillation prediction and reached up to 58% in precision.
assertions.anchor: Section IV Results and Discussion, p.5
quotes: providing a performance increase of at least 40% over the baseline GB model
improvements exceeding 100% in recall for atrial fibrillation prediction and up to 58% in precision for certain configurations
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study by the vendor's own team.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is to classical models on the same features, not to a classical simulation of the quench dynamics.

assertions.value: The authors state that their work presents the first quantum ML demonstrations at the quantum-advantage level.
quotes: Our work presents the first quantum ML demonstrations at the quantum-advantage level, bridging the gap between quantum supremacy and useful real-world academic and industrial applications.
assertions.certainty_reason: A company describing its own result in the abstract.
assertions.reader_inference: In the sections read, the evidence is better scores than classical ML baselines; no argument is seen that a classical method cannot match the features.

assertions.value: The authors give test set sizes of 398 samples for the atrial fibrillation task and 40 samples for the molecular toxicity task when interpreting recall gains.
assertions.anchor: Section IV Results and Discussion, p.5
quotes: a 24% increase in recall on a test set of 398 samples
a 25% increase in recall on a test set of 40 samples
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state their own test set sizes.
assertions.reader_inference: A test set of 40 samples is small for a percentage-gain claim.

assertions.value: The authors report empirically that ML models benefit most from feature representations obtained in the fast coherent regime of a quantum annealer, particularly near the critical point of the quantum dynamics.
quotes: ML models benefit most from feature representations obtained in the fast coherent regime of a quantum annealer, particularly near the critical point of the quantum dynamics
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

papers.title_in_file: An Independent Implementation of Quantum Machine Learning Algorithms in Qiskit for Genomic Data
papers.what_it_is: A three-page preliminary report implementing QSVC, Pegasos-QSVC, VQC and QNN in Qiskit for genomic sequence classification.

assertions.value: The authors describe preliminary work that implements and evaluates QSVC, PegasosQSVC, VQC and QNN algorithms in Qiskit with different feature maps, on a subset of 100,000 genome sequences with four qubits.
quotes: In this preliminary research, we employ feature mapping techniques: ZFeatureMap, ZZFeatureMap, and PauliFeatureMap
A subset of 100,000 genome sequences (divided into training and test sets) is selected for analysis to evaluate various QML models.
in our experiments using four qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2 states the experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors report substantial improvement over prior works [1], [2] and [5] in train and test accuracy, precision, recall, F1-Score and AUROC, as shown in Table 1.
quotes: Our detailed evaluation with classification metrics is shown in Table 1, illustrating substantial improvement compared to [1], [2] and [5] in accuracies (train and test), precision, recall, F1-Score, and AUROC
assertions.certainty_reason: An author-reported empirical result; the Table 1 values are not in the extracted text.
assertions.reader_inference: No numbers appear in the extracted text, so the size of the improvement cannot be checked here.

assertions.value: The authors state that their analysis is preliminary and that further detailed investigation with larger datasets is needed.
quotes: Although our preliminary analysis demonstrates improved performance, ongoing detailed investigations
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated by the authors in the conclusion.

papers.title_in_file: Optimised Hybrid Classical-Quantum Algorithm for Accelerated Solution of Sparse Linear Systems
papers.what_it_is: A single-author paper combining CUDA preconditioning, the HHL algorithm run on a quantum simulator, and a learned parameter selector for sparse linear systems.

assertions.value: The author reports that CUDA-accelerated preconditioning achieved speedups of up to 15x over CPU implementations and that the hybrid algorithm outperformed classical-only methods by up to 10x for larger system sizes.
quotes: CUDA-accelerated preconditioning achieved speedups of up to 15x compared to CPU implementations.
The hybrid algorithm outperformed classical-only methods by up to 10x for larger system sizes.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single-author empirical result; the matrix sizes and baselines are not given in the extracted text.
assertions.reader_inference: The quantum step ran on a simulator, so the 10x total-time figure is not evidence of a quantum speedup.

assertions.value: The author states the experiments used an NVIDIA GPU for classical processing and a quantum simulator for the HHL algorithm.
quotes: classical processing (CUDA) and a quantum simulator for the HHL
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 5.1 states the setup.

assertions.value: The author states the algorithm is limited by the current state of quantum hardware, with real-world implementation on actual quantum devices challenging due to limited qubits and high error rates.
quotes: Despite its advantages, the algorithm is limited by the current state of quantum hardware.
real-world implementation on actual quantum devices remains challenging due to limited qubits and high error rates
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 6.2 states the limit.

papers.title_in_file: Benchmarking MedMNIST dataset on real quantum hardware
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Section 3 hardware inference results and comparison with classical models, Section 4 conclusion; circuit-generation and ablation details skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A benchmark of quantum-only classifiers on the MedMNIST medical image datasets, trained on classical hardware and run on a 127-qubit IBM device with error mitigation.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the 2-class PneumoniaMNIST dataset their QML model obtained an AUC of 82.2% and an accuracy of 85.4% on IBM hardware, using at most 1000 test samples for datasets with many test samples.
quotes: For the 2-class PneumoniaMNIST dataset, we obtained good AUC and classification accuracies of 82.2% and 85.4% respectively.
Due to hardware limitations, we considered 1000 testing samples to evaluate the QML models for the datasets having a large number of testing samples.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on one device.

assertions.value: The authors state that their QML results do not outperform the best-performing classical ML model, and that the classical models use the full spatial dimensions of the images while the QML model uses a significantly reduced feature set.
quotes: Although the classification results obtained by our QML workflow do not outperform the best-performing classical ML model due to the inherent limitations of current NISQ hardware
All classical ML models leverage the full spatial dimensions of input images, whereas our QML model operates on a significantly reduced feature set, dictated by quantum hardware constraints.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit in Section 3.

assertions.value: The authors claim they achieve quantum advantage in both classification performance and computational complexity on RetinaMNIST when classical baselines use the same number of input features.
quotes: we achieve quantum advantage both in classification performance and computational complexity compared to classical ML baselines when evaluated on the RetinaMNIST dataset using the same number of input features
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim in the conclusion, limited to one dataset and a matched feature count.
assertions.reader_inference: The claim sits beside the authors' own statement that QML does not outperform the best classical model, so it holds only under the matched-feature condition.

assertions.value: The authors report that on hardware without error suppression and mitigation, accuracy and AUC on OCTMNIST fell by 15.70% and 11.40% compared with noiseless results.
quotes: For the OCTMNIST dataset, the classification accuracy and AUC on the hardware (without error suppression and mitigation) are reduced by 15.70% and 11.40% respectively as compared to the noiseless results.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on one device.
